extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, political scientists, policymakers, and students studying media economics and news markets
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and empirical guidance for analyzing how economic forces (owners' motivations, technology, property rights, and market structure) shape news content and how content may translate into political consequences. Includes measurement strategies (product differentiation, search and consumption patterns) and empirical proxies for hard vs soft news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-demand questions for story selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Who cares about a particular piece of information? What are they willing to pay to find it, or what are others willing to pay to reach them? Where can media outlets or advertisers reach these people? When is it profitable to provide the information? Why is this profitable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these five economic questions as the ultimate determinants of what emerges as news: they shape editors' and producers' choices, images selected, audiences/advertisers attracted, and which outlets survive. Use them as primary evaluative dimensions when assessing why stories are (or are not) produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public goods nature of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is a public good: one person's consumption doesn't preclude another's and once information circulates it can be consumed without paying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect underproduction of certain public affairs information because private incentives may not cover social returns; measure spillovers and the ease with which one outlet's discovery can be used by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as experience goods and signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: News is an experience good — consumers must consume to learn its quality; firms use signals (brand names, celebrity journalists) so consumers can anticipate content without sampling each item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reputation-building (brands, anchors, pundits) as a mechanism for reducing buyer uncertainty; consider how journalist celebrity becomes part of the product and affects content expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: High fixed costs / low variable costs
rubrics_metrics.description: News production involves high fixed costs (reporters, production technology) and low marginal costs (additional copies or server space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess market structure implications: high fixed costs limit number of viable providers; economies of scale shape incentives for content mix and entry/exit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product differentiation and spatial product location
rubrics_metrics.description: Providers distinguish their version of news and tailor content to particular consumer interests; product positioning predicts the mix of hard and soft news in a market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spatial models to predict and measure variety (e.g., niche soft-news channels vs broad hard-news outlets); expect more differentiation as markets consolidate or as the number of channels increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational ignorance of political information
rubrics_metrics.description: Because an individual voter's actions are unlikely to be decisive, the expected private benefit of learning detailed politics is small, so citizens often remain rationally ignorant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret low demand for public affairs content as partly endogenous to rational cost–benefit calculations; this explains divergence between information people want vs need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser valuation and audience targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Content choices are influenced by which audience segments advertisers value (e.g., younger females command higher ad premiums), leading outlets to target those demographics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating content, measure advertiser willingness-to-pay by audience segment and check whether story selection targets advertiser-valued demographics (example: networks covering issues important to women 18–34).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard news vs soft news distinction and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard news (government, policy, major events) vs soft news (human interest, entertainment); economic incentives (costs, advertiser value, audience tastes) determine the relative provision of hard and soft news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize hard/soft categories (see empirical proxies) and assess how costs, audience composition, and advertiser preferences shift the balance toward soft news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owners' motivations and conglomerate incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: The motivations of media outlet owners (profit maximization, political goals, cross-ownership interests) influence content choices, including favoring owned content over competitors'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine ownership structure, corporate incentives, and cross-ownership ties to detect systematic content biases or conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology and distribution environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Available dissemination technologies (number of channels, cable, Internet) change expected audience size and enable niche programming; more channels permit profitable niche (ideological or soft-news) outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how technological changes alter audience fragmentation, niche entry, and the feasibility of targeted content (e.g., Fox News emergence as niche conservative channel because households receive many channels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property rights and regulatory environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Property rights (copyright law) and regulations (e.g., Fairness Doctrine) affect incentives to produce controversial or public-affairs programming and influence the supply of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how regulatory constraints or protections change the costs/benefits of hard news production and the chilling or enabling effects on content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of product differentiation, search patterns, and consumption patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Three suggested types of analyses to test how competition influences content: measurement of product differentiation, of information search patterns, and of consumption patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design empirical strategies around these three analyses: (a) map variety/positioning across outlets; (b) study what users search for online or in print (search behavior); (c) analyze actual consumption (readership, viewing, linking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational proxies for hard/soft news
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete proxies to define hard vs soft news: e.g., People magazine lists for soft news; law review compilations of major Supreme Court cases, Congressional Quarterly key votes, and interest-group ratings for hard news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding content, adopt transparent proxy lists (People for soft, CQ and law-review cases for hard) to ensure replicability and to track coverage trends over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative empirical methods and proxies
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical methods include contingent valuation (willingness-to-pay), analysis of cable subscription prices, product positioning studies, linking activity on the Internet, and measures of beat types and product variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select appropriate economic and observational measures (e.g., cable prices to infer average willingness-to-pay for networks; People/Time subscriptions to infer soft/hard news interest) and triangulate across methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness of coverage to incidence vs reader interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage may be driven either by actual local incidence (e.g., prevalence of an issue) or by reader interest; effects vary by topic (some hard-news topics respond to incidence; crime coverage may respond more to reader interest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating coverage adequacy, compare real-world incidence data with frequency/intensity of coverage to detect under- or over-provision relative to local needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branding and celebrity as a content-stabilizing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Transforming journalists into celebrities helps consumers form expectations about content and reduces uncertainty about product quality in crowded markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the degree to which outlets promote journalist-branding (anchor salaries, pundit visibility) and evaluate its effect on audience retention and content style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium effects on content and pundit behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Pundits and journalists strategically alter language and focus depending on medium: e.g., on television they emphasize entertainment values, use less abstract terms, and tailor ideology/language to audience expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the same journalist across media to detect medium-driven shifts; consider how these shifts affect informational content and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet's mixed impact and audience concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet expands access to high-quality news but rational ignorance persists online; advertisers pay more for product/entertainment-related search results, and linking activity concentrates traffic (top outlets garner disproportionately large shares).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both supply-side expansion (more availability) and demand-side concentration (top sites dominating traffic), and measure search behavior to see whether users seek hard or soft content.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of potential market failures in news markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems include: underconsumption of public-affairs news; inadequate investment in hard news; bias against high-cost news that benefits minorities; tilt toward advertiser-valued information; need to create celebrity brands; conduit owners favoring own content; journalist herding; conglomerates focusing solely on profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to diagnose market failures present in a given media market and to prioritize which failures are most damaging given local context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs in intellectual property policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard-to-predict balance between strong copyright (which encourages production) and less stringent protection (which favors dissemination and consumption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate copyright policy by weighing production incentives against dissemination/externality benefits and by empirical assessment of how protections affect output and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenges in linking content to political consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Key identification problems: verifying exposure (who 'gets the news'), measuring consumed content, establishing baseline opinions, disentangling media effects from confounding real-world events, and dealing with endogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lab experiments, Internet experiments, panel survey reinterviews, and careful design to isolate causal chains (exposure -> opinion/behavior -> political outcomes). Explicitly document assumptions about timing, voter responsiveness, and shortcuts (party ID) used by voters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frameworks for assessing media effects (agenda-setting, framing, priming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominent mechanisms by which media influence politics: agenda setting (defining important issues), framing (how issues are described), and priming (defining criteria for evaluating officials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating political impact of content, test for these mechanisms using content measures and outcome variables; consider decay curves and audience segmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical indicators of market structure effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators include owner concentration, number of beat types covered, product variety, readership penetration (e.g., New York Times penetration) and its spillover effects on local papers and civic participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure concentration and diversity metrics; evaluate whether consolidation increases differentiation (e.g., more beat types) or reduces public-affairs provision in specific contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of observational and experimental methods to identify effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods recommended: content analysis (longitudinal), lab framing experiments, Internet experiments, contingent valuation, price-based inference, and panel survey analysis to infer causal effects of content on attitudes and turnout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine observational and experimental approaches where possible; explicitly address selection into exposure and use reinterview/panel data or randomized exposures to strengthen causal claims.
